summary: Electronic health records (EHRs) are central to patient-centered care. However, many current EHR systems do not represent, exchange, or reuse genomic findings in structured, interoperable, and clinically actionable forms. Instead, genomic results are often retained in static reports. This limits their use in routine clinical care and clinical decision support. It also restricts their future reinterpretation as scientific knowledge evolves, as well as their reuse for research within appropriate governance frameworks. To support precision and personalized medicine, we advocate that clinically relevant genomic findings should be represented within EHRs as structured, phenotype-linked, interoperable, and versioned data. Raw and intermediate genomic files, however, should remain in appropriately governed laboratory or genomics repositories. This viewpoint is intended for health policymakers, health informatics leaders, EHR developers, research and clinical genomics laboratories, and clinicians involved in implementing genomics into routine care. It is informed by selected published literature and relevant technical standards. It is also informed by operational experience at the Cyprus Institute of Neurology and Genetics and multidisciplinary discussions from the Gen2EHR Implementation Guidelines Workshop conducted within the Extended EHR@EU Data Space and European Health Data Space for Secondary Use @CY initiatives. We examine technical, organizational, clinical, ethical, legal, and governance challenges, including inconsistent reporting formats and unclear clinical responsibility. We propose a staged, workshop-informed implementation pathway for evaluation within the European Health Data Space. The pathway combines Health Level 7 Fast Health Interoperability Resources Genomics Reporting with complementary standards and terminologies. It also includes transitional dual PDF and structured Fast Health Interoperability Resources reporting, governance for access, version control, reinterpretation, and clinical responsibility, as well as multidisciplinary pilot validation in real diagnostic workflows. The clinical effectiveness and transferability of the proposed pathway across European health systems remain to be established.
title: Making Genomic Data Actionable in Electronic Health Records: Practical Viewpoint on Standards, Governance, and Implementation

summary: Background: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) aims to optimize clinical outcomes but is hindered by logistical delays and susceptibility to data errors. Integrating model-informed precision dosing with point-of-care testing, fortified by rule-based validation and alerts, forms a transformative clinical decision support system (CDSS) essential for securing this complex workflow. Objective: This study evaluates, , the effectiveness of a rule-based CDSS for imatinib in detecting data-quality issues and optimizing therapeutic dosing, compared with a human TDM expert. Methods: We simulated a set of 60 virtual patients using a previously developed population pharmacokinetic model and deliberately enriched it with data-quality errors (eg, timing inaccuracies and reporting errors) to stress-test system resilience. We compared CDSS and TDM expert performances based on their error-detection capabilities and the clinical impact on therapeutic target attainment and safety. Results: The CDSS and the expert demonstrated comparable error-detection capabilities. The CDSS showed numerically higher sensitivity (53%, 95% CI 35%‐70% vs 45%, 95% CI 30%‐61%) and lower specificity (83%, 95% CI 63%‐95% vs 100%, 95% CI 81%‐100%). Clinically, the CDSS demonstrated significantly higher rates of target attainment than the expert (33/60, 55% vs 22/60, 37%; =.046). However, the CDSS resulted in 5 detrimental outcomes against 1 for the TDM expert, in which patients initially within the target range fell outside it. Conclusions: The CDSS demonstrated high efficacy in optimizing imatinib exposure while serving as a robust digital gatekeeper. While active optimization drives higher efficacy, a few observed detrimental cases highlight that algorithmic safety remains contingent on data integrity. This proof-of-concept study validates the CDSS architecture as a prerequisite for future prospective clinical trials.
title: Safety and Performance Evaluation of a Clinical Decision Support System for Imatinib Therapeutic Drug Monitoring: In Silico Study

summary: Background: Cross-domain chest radiograph report generation may produce formally valid reports that are nevertheless repetitive, weakly case-specific, or missing clinically relevant findings. These failures can be missed when evaluation relies on a single language-overlap or clinical-label score. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate cross-domain report generation with a bidirectional layered audit, characterize direction-specific and end point–specific failure profiles under a composite training-side control and 3 decoding policies, and explore whether selected audit dimensions remained informative for a contemporary medical vision language model. Methods: A fixed R2Gen-style system was evaluated bidirectionally on 575 IU X-ray and 401 MIMIC-CXR (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care Chest X-Ray) target records. The audit included surface validity, complete-report recurrence and concentration, a predefined prefix end point, lexical diversity, official Stanford CheXpert/NegBio labels, paired cluster-bootstrap inference, and blinded review by 2 medical trainees. The primary human audit included 210 reports from 70 randomly sampled cases, with blinded adjudication of unresolved primary end point disagreements. A 60-report targeted panel was used for failure-mode analysis. Separately, a fixed MedGemma 1.5 4B configuration generated reports for all 976 records. Results: In MIMIC-CXR–to–IU X-ray transfer, out of 575 reports, ON (protocol-defined training-side control enabled)+B4 (beam search with a beam size of 4) reduced the predefined recurrent prefix from 575 (100%) to 8 (1.4%; Holm-adjusted =.002). However, 569 (99.0%) ON+B4 outputs still belonged to exact duplicate groups. In IU X-ray–to–MIMIC-CXR transfer, the 14-category CheXpert/NegBio micro- was higher for ON+B4 than for OFF (protocol-defined training-side control disabled)+B4 (0.1687 vs 0.0744; Holm-adjusted =.01). This apparent advantage was not broad-based: after cardiomegaly was excluded in a post hoc descriptive sensitivity analysis, the difference changed from +0.0944 to −0.0610. Text-level tracing showed that the original contrast was mainly driven by a labeler response to recurrent, semantically normal heart-size wording. Across the primary human-audit cells, major omissions occurred in 12 to 15 out of 35 reports, and major unsupported findings occurred in 10 to 16 of 35 reports, with no consistent configuration ordering observed. The exploratory MedGemma micro- was 0.4722 on IU X-ray and 0.4340 on MIMIC-CXR, but 381 out of 575 (66.3%) IU outputs belonged to exact duplicate groups. Conclusions: No configuration performed consistently well across end points, and no single metric captured all forms of cross-domain degradation. The MedGemma stress test suggested that recurrence and label-traceability checks remain useful across architectures, although it was not a matched performance comparison. Cross-domain report generators should undergo bidirectional evaluation, final-text verification, and image-grounded human review before external validation or clinical deployment.
title: Cross-Domain Chest Radiograph Report Generation Under Dataset Shift: Bidirectional Audit Study

summary: This letter comments on two aspects of the study by Lin et al. We discuss how agreement in ordinal ASA classification is reported and how disagreements across ASA classes could be presented more clearly. We also address the uncertainty around the change in agreement after adding National Health Insurance data.
title: Interpreting Agreement in AI-Assisted American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Classification
Authors' Reply: Interpreting Agreement in AI-Assisted American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Classification

summary: Background: The development of structured optical character recognition (OCR) systems for Korean medical documents is hindered by strict privacy regulations that limit access to real clinical data. Existing synthetic document frameworks are primarily designed for generic layouts and Western languages, and fail to capture the complex formatting, bilingual terminology, and hierarchical field semantics required for clinical OCR and document-understanding tasks in hospital environments. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a privacy-preserving, template-driven pipeline for generating realistic synthetic Korean medical documents with structured XML annotations, enabling OCR and document-understanding model training in settings where access to real clinical data is restricted. Methods: We designed MedDocSynth, a 7-stage synthetic document generation pipeline that reconstructs authentic medical document layouts from publicly available references, incorporates clinician-guided template selection, and uses a structured placeholder system encoding 17 medical data types. Human-curated templates were populated with exemplar content and tagged using a delimiter-based scheme, after which GPT-4o-mini generated diverse synthetic values for each field. The pipeline produced 1000 fully synthetic DOCX documents with corresponding XML annotations encoding hierarchical structure, title-answer relationships, and datatype metadata. We evaluated text fidelity, lexical diversity (type-token ratio, measure of textual lexical diversity [MTLD], n-grams, and Pareto), and compared the system with existing synthetic document pipelines. A Qwen2.5-VL model was fine-tuned exclusively on the synthetic dataset and evaluated on 50 real-world Korean clinical documents to assess OCR accuracy, information extraction, and table reconstruction. Results: The pipeline achieved 100% placeholder coverage, 99.68% format correctness, and 91.56% semantic accuracy. Lexical diversity analysis demonstrated high variability in free-text fields (MTLD≈456) and expected repetitiveness in structured datatypes. Compared with existing pipelines (SynthText, SynthTiger, and DocSynth), the proposed system uniquely supports complex clinical forms, bilingual content, and structured XML annotations. When trained solely on the synthetic data, Qwen2.5-VL achieved the highest real-world performance, with a character accuracy of 86.01%, word accuracy of 78.25%, field accuracy of 67.18%, datatype accuracy of 64.14%, and table reconstruction tree-edit-distance similarity score of 71.09%. Models without fine-tuning performed substantially worse, including GPT-5-mini. Conclusions: We present the first synthetic data generation pipeline specifically tailored to Korean medical documents, enabling the creation of realistic, richly annotated datasets for structured OCR without exposing patient information. The synthetic data significantly improves OCR performance on real clinical documents, demonstrating the pipeline’s potential utility for hospital deployment and its potential extensibility to other languages and health care systems.
title: Synthetic Medical Document Generation Pipeline (MedDocSynth) for Optical Character Recognition: Development and Validation Study on Korean Clinical Documents

summary: Background: Health AI investment is accelerating across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), yet the region’s health AI research output has never been systematically quantified. National research capacity is a structural precondition for the safe local development and governance of clinical AI, but no scientometric baseline exists for the 6 GCC states. Objective: We characterized the volume, growth, collaboration structure, and thematic composition of GCC health AI research and examined whether national output aligns with an existing measure of informatics readiness. Methods: We conducted an ecological scientometric analysis of all health AI publications affiliated with the 6 GCC states (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates) for 2011 to 2024 (the last complete indexing year at extraction) using the open bibliographic database OpenAlex. A publication was eligible if it included both an AI family and a health or medicine family concept above a 0.30 relevance threshold. Bibliometric indicators (output, compound annual growth, per capita intensity, citation impact, international and intraregional collaboration, and institutional concentration) were computed; coauthorship and concept co-occurrence networks were constructed and clustered by modularity. National health AI intensity was correlated (Spearman) with the Health Informatics Readiness Index (HIRI) and Global Digital Health Monitor (GDHM) phase. Results: Of 112,480 GCC-affiliated AI publications, 3512 met the health AI definition. Regional output rose from 18 (2011) to 904 (2024) publications per year (compound annual growth=35.2%), with 86.4% (3034/3512) published from 2020 onward and a sharp inflection from 2019 to 2021. Saudi Arabia contributed 59.6% (2094/3512) of the output by itself and 81.5% (2862/3512) together with the United Arab Emirates; Qatar led on a per capita basis (approximately 136 publications per million population). International collaboration (2551/3512, 72.6% of the papers) predominated over intra-GCC collaboration (164/3327, 4.9%), with the latter being inversely related to national output. The principal external partners were India, the United States, Pakistan, the United Kingdom, and Egypt. Output spanned 3186 institutions; concentration ranged from 89.4% (328/367) of a country’s output among the top 3 institutions for Qatar to 34.4% (721/2094) for Saudi Arabia. Concept co-occurrence was classified into 4 themes—classic machine learning clinical prediction, medical imaging and oncology, COVID-19 response, and diabetic eye disease. Health AI intensity (ρ=+0.60) and, more strongly, absolute output (ρ=+0.89) correlated with the HIRI; absolute output was also correlated with GDHM phase (ρ=+0.83). Conclusions: GCC health AI research has grown rapidly but unevenly, is heavily dependent on international collaboration, is concentrated in medical imaging, and—outside Saudi Arabia—remains anchored in single national institutions. Informatics readiness was associated with both the intensity and the volume of national research output. The findings establish a reproducible baseline for monitoring regional health AI research capacity as GCC health systems move toward clinical AI deployment.
title: Capacity, Collaboration, and Thematic Structure in Health AI Research Over the Past Decade in the Gulf Cooperation Council: Scientometric Analysis

summary: Background: Summary care records are digital technologies designed to support information sharing and care coordination across fragmented health and social care systems. However, adoption and use of these technologies can vary across diverse health and care settings, with users using workarounds and other strategies to meet their specific information needs. In Scotland, the Key Information Summary (KIS) has been in use for over 13 years, sharing key patient information from general practitioners (GPs) with other health and care providers for future care planning. Objective: Using the KIS as a case study, this study examines how various adoption strategies and workarounds have shaped the evolution of regional information infrastructures integrating health and social care in Scotland over time. Methods: This multimethod qualitative study examined the various contextual factors influencing adoption and use of the KIS across diverse health and care settings. Data collection included interviews with KIS users from health and care settings, implementers, and vendors; documentary analysis of user guides, websites, reports, and policies; and observation of multidisciplinary team meetings and technology use. Data analysis involved a hybrid approach. The technology-people-organization-macroenvironment framework was applied to code interview, documentary, and observational data, followed by an inductive analysis informed by science and technology studies theories of information infrastructures, domestication, and workarounds to examine strategies and workarounds for adapting the KIS to local contexts and evolving needs. Results: Data comprised 54 qualitative interviews, 59 documents, 2 websites, and 20 hours of observational field notes collected between April 2024 and March 2025. Findings indicate that adoption of the KIS varied across settings and over time due to misalignment between system design, evolving expectations of integrated care, and national initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic that repurposed its use. Professional roles and associated information needs shaped differing expectations of what constituted useful information, generating tensions between users who relied on the KIS and GPs responsible for maintaining it. Formal workarounds enabled the extension of the health care–centric infrastructure into nonclinical settings to facilitate information sharing with GPs and, in some cases, supported clinician access to the KIS during system outages. Across settings, informal user-driven repair practices enabled diverse professionals to adopt and realign the KIS with its intended use. Conclusions: This study demonstrates how regional information infrastructures integrating health and care evolve incrementally as they become embedded within local routines, practices, and existing systems. Adoption was shaped by professional roles, information needs, and users’ capabilities, with formal workarounds extending infrastructures into new settings and informal, user-driven repair practices supporting ongoing use and maintenance. Policymakers and vendors must recognize that workarounds and user-driven repair practices are central to infrastructural growth and sustainability, and understanding these strategies can inform future technology development and innovation.
title: Adoption Strategies and Workarounds in the Evolution of Information Infrastructures Integrating Health and Social Care Providers in Scotland: Multimethod Qualitative Case Study of the Key Information Summary

summary: Background: Clinicians spend a lot of time on electronic health record (EHR) documentation, often at the expense of direct patient interaction. Ambient listening technology uses AI to passively record and summarize clinical encounters. Although early studies are promising, there is limited evidence on system performance in complex, non-English settings. Objective: This study aimed to compare the documentation performance of 3 commercially available ambient listening systems in simulated Dutch-language outpatient consultations by assessing note completeness, correctness, and conciseness under predefined linguistic and interactional challenges. Methods: Standardized audio recordings of 10 scripted physician-patient interactions across 2 specialties were used. Scenarios included multispeaker dynamics (patient companion), conversational disruptions (nurse interruption), evasive patient communication, and a regional dialect (Gronings). Three ambient listening providers (provider 1, provider 2, and provider 3) processed the audio files. Generated notes were divided into 4 note sections: patient history, physical examination, diagnostic impression, and treatment plan. For each system output, each note section was scored for completeness, conciseness, and correctness using a 5-point ordinal scale against physician-developed reference summaries. In total, 8 clinicians participated in scoring: 4 junior clinicians evaluated all outputs, and 4 senior clinicians each reviewed a subset of scenarios. Analyses were based on 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores. Interrater agreement was assessed using Gwet agreement coefficient 2 (Gwet AC-2). System-level technical characteristics were assessed alongside clinical performance to aid interpretation of between-provider differences. Results: Across 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores on a 5-point scale, overall interrater agreement was high (Gwet AC-2=0.827). Provider-level mean scores ranged from 3.82 to 4.26 (4.26, SD 0.73 for provider 3, 4.00, SD 0.90 for provider 2, and 3.82, SD 1.07 for provider 1). Mean scores were higher in otolaryngology than in surgical oncology (4.36, SD 0.56 vs 3.68, SD 1.10). Across scoring domains, correctness received the highest mean score (4.21, SD 0.98), while completeness received the lowest (3.81, SD 0.90). Variation in mean scores was observed across script scenarios. Dialect-containing scenarios had the lowest mean score overall (3.77, SD 1.21), although this pattern was not uniform across specialties and systems. Median summary generation times ranged from 13.5 seconds (IQR 12-15; provider 3) to 22.0 seconds (IQR 18-24; provider 2). Conclusions: Ambient listening systems demonstrated generally strong performance in this simulated Dutch-language evaluation, including under several common conversational challenges. However, mean scores varied across scripted scenarios, with lower scores observed in some dialect-containing and otherwise challenging interactions. Future deployment studies must prioritize linguistic equity, real-world validation of efficiency gains, and evaluation of both clinician and patient perceptions to understand how these systems influence consultation dynamics and care delivery across diverse patient populations.
title: Three Ambient Listening Systems in Simulated Dutch-Language Multispeaker and Multidialect Clinical Encounters: Comparative Study

summary: Background: Regulatory frameworks such as the Belmont Report, the Common Rule, and the Declaration of Helsinki require informed consent to ensure participants understand a study’s purpose and can make voluntary decisions about their involvement. Regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation [EU] 2016/679), further emphasize that consent must be freely given and revocable without disadvantage. Although informed consent forms (ICFs) are intended to be clear and accessible, they have become increasingly lengthy and complex. Large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to navigate and interpret this complexity and have shown promise in biomedical information extraction tasks. However, their susceptibility to hallucinations limits their reliability in high-stakes settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can mitigate such errors. Objective: This study evaluates the integration of GPT-4.1 with RAG for reviewing data reuse language in ICFs and its ability to interpret complex ICF language. Methods: First, we processed 438 ICFs from different trials, including multiple countries, languages, and versions of ICFs. Using expertly curated prompts, we extracted information about data reuse using GPT-4.1. By comparing the LLM-generated data reuse outputs with human expert ground truth, we evaluated accuracy and the time required to extract information for each ICF. To further validate the workflow, we evaluated an independent set of 488 ICFs spanning additional trials, languages, and regions. During the validation phase, the workflow was evaluated using a baseline assessment (89 ICFs) followed by 3 iterative optimization rounds assessed on 14, 281, and 104 ICFs, respectively. For this cohort, we assessed the correctness of LLM outputs along with the quality of supporting evidence provided by the model. Results: Across the initial set of 438 ICFs, the system achieved 81.6% accuracy. During validation, the baseline accuracy using the preoptimized prompts was 84.0% (89 documents). Accuracy improved sequentially across the 3 iterative optimization rounds, increasing from 82.3% in the first round (14 documents) to 90.7% in the second round (281 documents), and reaching 92.1% in the third and final round on an independent holdout cohort of 104 documents. Ultimately, using our RAG-based approach, the system accurately extracted data reuse information across multiple languages. Conclusions: Our RAG-based workflow demonstrated the ability to effectively support the ICF review process for data reuse and interpret complex consent language, contributing to improved consistency in ICF evaluations for data reuse.
title: Large Language Model–Assisted Review of Clinical Trial Informed Consent for Data Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach
